content: CD45, in the field of immunology, refers to a protein that was initially identified as the leukocyte common antigen. The term CD stands for cluster of differentiation. This protein is encoded by a gene that belongs to the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) family. PTPs are signaling molecules that play critical roles in regulating various cellular processes, including cell growth, differentiation, the mitotic cycle, and oncogenic transformation. The CD45 protein is characterized by its structure, which includes an extracellular domain, a single transmembrane segment, and two tandem intracellular catalytic domains. This structural composition classifies it as a receptor-type PTP. The gene encoding CD45 is specifically expressed in hematopoietic cells, and the protein is a crucial regulator of antigen receptor signaling in both T cells and B cells. It achieves this regulatory function either by directly interacting with components of the antigen receptor complexes or by activating various Src family kinases that are essential for antigen receptor signaling. Additionally, CD45 suppresses JAK kinases, thereby acting as a regulator of cytokine receptor signaling. The CD45 gene undergoes alternative splicing, resulting in four transcript variants that encode distinct isoforms. This protein is a type I transmembrane protein expressed in various forms on all differentiated hematopoietic cells, except for erythrocytes and plasma cells. CD45 plays a role in the activation of these cells, functioning as a co-stimulatory molecule. It is expressed in lymphomas, B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia, hairy cell leukemia, and acute non-lymphocytic leukemia. The CD45 family consists of multiple members, all of which are products of a single complex gene. This gene contains 34 exons, and three of these exons are alternatively spliced in the primary transcripts to generate up to eight different mature mRNAs. After translation, these mRNAs produce eight distinct protein products. The three alternatively spliced exons give rise to the RA, RB, and RC isoforms. Various isoforms of CD45 exist, including CD45RA, CD45RB, CD45RC, CD45RAB, CD45RAC, CD45RBC, CD45RO, and CD45R(ABC). CD45 is also highly glycosylated. The longest isoform, CD45R, migrates at 200 kDa when isolated from T cells. B cells also express CD45R, but with heavier glycosylation, which increases its molecular weight to 220 kDa, hence the designation B220. The B220 isoform is not restricted to B cells and can also be expressed on activated T cells, a subset of dendritic cells, and other antigen-presenting cells. Naive T lymphocytes express large CD45 isoforms and are typically positive for CD45RA. In contrast, activated and memory T lymphocytes express the shortest CD45 isoform, CD45RO, which lacks the RA, RB, and RC exons. This shorter isoform facilitates T cell activation. The cytoplasmic domain of CD45 is one of the largest known and possesses intrinsic phosphatase activity. This activity removes an inhibitory phosphate group from a tyrosine kinase, such as Lck in T cells or Syk in B cells, thereby activating these kinases.
